hypothesis: COG1760 (L-serine deaminase, amino acid transport and metabolism) is increased or characteristic in 12-month-old infants receiving meat-based complementary protein relative to dairy-based complementary protein.
rationale: No published study was found that reports COG1760 / L-serine deaminase (sdaA/sdaB-type L-serine ammonia-lyase) specifically as differentially abundant between meat- and dairy-fed infants. However, multiple converging lines of same-direction evidence exist at the pathway/category level and mechanistically. (1) A metagenomic/metabolomic analysis of a randomized controlled complementary feeding trial in U.S. formula-fed infants (meat vs. dairy protein, 5-12 months) reported that the meat-diet group was enriched for microbial genes in the COG category 'amino acid transport and metabolism' (FDR = 0.006) - the exact functional category to which COG1760 belongs - alongside nucleotide and carbohydrate metabolism enrichments. (2) A companion report from an infant complementary feeding cohort found that meat-derived nutrients at 9 months correlated strongly with increased microbiome amino acid metabolism/biosynthesis functions. (3) The parent trial reported meat-specific increases in amino-acid-fermenting Firmicutes (Ruminococcus, Roseburia) relative to dairy, consistent with a shift toward proteolytic/amino-acid catabolic capacity. (4) Basic microbiology establishes that L-serine deaminase abundance/activity is driven by luminal L-serine availability and that gut bacteria use it as a one-step, high-yield route from serine to pyruvate + ammonia, so greater delivery of animal protein-derived free/undigested amino acids to the distal gut plausibly selects for this gene family. Because the direct group-level evidence is category-level (not feature-specific) and comes from the same trial design rather than independent cohorts, this falls short of 'strong' but satisfies 'multiple indirect/pathway-level studies pointing the same direction'.
mechanism: L-serine deaminase (L-serine ammonia-lyase; SdaA/SdaB homologs, COG1760) catabolizes L-serine to pyruvate and ammonia in a single ATP-efficient step, letting gut bacteria use serine as a carbon/energy and nitrogen source and contributing to acid/stress tolerance. Meat-based complementary feeding increases the flux of animal protein and peptide/amino-acid substrate reaching the colon relative to a dairy-based diet, while shifting the community away from milk-oligosaccharide/lactose-driven saccharolytic Bifidobacterium toward amino-acid- and fiber-fermenting Clostridia (Roseburia, Ruminococcus) and Enterobacteriaceae that carry serine catabolic operons. Substrate-driven selection and induction of serine utilization genes would therefore raise the metagenomic abundance of COG1760 in the meat group by 12 months.

evidence.title: Network-based representation learning reveals the impact of age and diet on the gut microbial and metabolomic environment of U.S. infants in a randomized controlled feeding trial
evidence.study_population: U.S. formula-fed infants, 5-12 months, randomized controlled complementary feeding trial (meat- vs. dairy-based protein); fecal shotgun metagenomics + metabolomics
evidence.relevance: Most direct evidence: reports that microbial features classified to the meat-diet group were significantly enriched for the COG functional category 'amino acid transport and metabolism' (FDR=0.006), the category containing COG1760, supporting the hypothesized direction at pathway/category level in exactly this exposure group and age window.

evidence.title: Protein Intake During Early Complementary Feeding Affects the Gut Microbiota in U.S. Formula-fed Infants (FS04-03-19)
evidence.study_population: Healthy term U.S. formula-fed infants randomized to meat- or dairy-based complementary protein, followed to 12 months
evidence.relevance: Primary trial report showing meat-specific increases in amino-acid/protein-fermenting genera (Ruminococcus, Roseburia; significant group-by-time interaction) versus dairy, i.e. a taxonomic shift compatible with greater serine-catabolic gene capacity in the meat group at 12 months, though serine deaminase itself was not measured.

evidence.title: Connecting Infant Complementary Feeding Patterns with Microbiome Development
evidence.study_population: Infants sampled at ~6, 9 and 12 months during complementary feeding; shotgun metagenomics and global metabolite profiling with diet records
evidence.relevance: Reports that nutrients from meat products at 9 months correlated strongly (canonical correlation >=0.6) with increased microbiome amino acid metabolism and biosynthesis functions, corroborating a meat-associated increase in amino-acid metabolic gene content of which L-serine deaminase is one component.

evidence.title: Dietary l-serine confers a competitive fitness advantage to Enterobacteriaceae in the inflamed gut
evidence.study_population: Mouse models colonized with E. coli LF82 and Citrobacter rodentium; dietary L-serine manipulation
evidence.relevance: Indirect mechanistic support that luminal (dietary) L-serine availability drives selection for bacterial L-serine utilization/catabolic genes, the pathway represented by COG1760, linking dietary protein-derived serine supply to serine deaminase-dependent fitness.

evidence.title: Serine Deamination Is a New Acid Tolerance Mechanism Observed in Uropathogenic Escherichia coli
evidence.study_population: In vitro bacterial genetics (uropathogenic E. coli UTI89, sdaA/sdaB deletion mutants)
evidence.relevance: Establishes the enzymatic function and physiological role of the SdaA/SdaB L-serine deaminases (COG1760 family): import of exogenous L-serine via SdaC and deamination to pyruvate, supporting substrate-driven relevance of this gene family in the gut lumen.

evidence.title: Increased dietary protein stimulates amino acid catabolism via the gut microbiota and secondary bile acid production
evidence.study_population: Dietary protein dose-response feeding intervention with gut microbiota and host amino acid catabolic enzyme profiling (animal/mammalian model per report; not infants)
evidence.relevance: Indirect support that higher dietary protein intake up-regulates amino acid catabolism involving the gut microbiota, including serine-degrading enzyme activity (serine dehydratase among the amino acid degrading enzymes increased), consistent with increased serine deamination capacity on a meat/high-animal-protein diet.

contradicting_evidence: No study was found reporting L-serine deaminase or serine catabolic genes higher in dairy-fed than meat-fed infants, so no direct contradiction. Two tempering observations: (a) the same meat-vs-dairy infant trial analysis noted that conventional differential abundance testing of individual features found no significant diet associations (the meat/amino-acid signal emerged only from the network-embedding approach), so feature-level significance for genes like COG1760 is not established; (b) dairy proteins (casein/whey) are themselves serine-rich, and a murine metatranscriptomic study of milk-protein fermentation shows milk protein also fuels microbial amino acid fermentation, so a dairy-driven increase in serine catabolic gene expression cannot be excluded.

caveats: Key caveat: the strongest supporting source is a preprint analysis of a meat-vs-dairy infant feeding trial that very likely uses the same or a closely related cohort/dataset as the present study, so it is not an independent replication and its support is at the COG-category level ('amino acid transport and metabolism'), not for COG1760 specifically. The related 9-month correlation report also derives from the same complementary feeding cohort. Remaining evidence is mechanistic/indirect (E. coli and Pseudomonas SdaA/SdaB biochemistry, mouse dietary L-serine studies, general protein-fermentation literature) and not infant- or diet-arm-specific. COG1760 also encompasses multiple bacterial serine/threonine ammonia-lyase homologs with different taxonomic carriers (Enterobacteriaceae, Clostridia, Bacteroides), so shifts in its abundance may reflect taxonomic turnover during weaning rather than diet-specific serine substrate availability. Finally, gene abundance does not equal serine catabolic flux; paired fecal serine/pyruvate or ammonia measurements would be needed to confirm functional relevance.
